title: Adaptive sequential baselines for CI perf regression detector
creator: Sofia Martinez
description:
Goal: Add an adaptive, statistically-sound regression detector to CI that gates PRs when relevant performance regressions appear. The detector must track tokens/sec and p95 latency (and surface the p99 when available), support per-model and per-sequence-length baselines, and minimize false positives from noise produced by infra variance or non-deterministic workloads.

Scope:
- Build a baseline runner that executes representative microbenchmarks per-commit and nightly.
- Implement sequential hypothesis testing (SPRT) with configurable alpha/beta defaults and an empirical noise model.
- Integrate detector into PR CI so failing tests produce clear actionable artifacts (histograms, raw traces, runner config, container image hash).
- Provide an opt-in non-blocking mode (warn-only) for new model integrations and a blocking mode for protected branches.

Design decisions and trade-offs:
1) Sequential test vs fixed-sample t-test: sequential tests allow early stopping and lower sample cost for large regressions, reducing CI runtime. We chose SPRT (Wald) with a conservative default to bound false-positive rate; preserve ability to switch to Bayesian change-point detection if we need richer posterior outputs.
2) Per-model stratified baselines: performance noise differs by model, tokenizer, and max-seq; baselines stored per (model, quantization, gpu-type, seq-bucket). This increases baseline storage but reduces type-I errors.
3) Tokens/sec and p95: tokens/sec is the primary throughput metric for cost regressions; p95 captures latency tail regressions that impact UX. We compute both and trigger on either metric passing a regression significance threshold.
4) CI cost vs sensitivity: To keep PR CI latency reasonable, we run a minimal sequential runner in PRs (N_min=5, N_max=40) sampling the most-representative batch sizes. Nightly baseline runs execute larger, more robust samples for longer-term baselining.

Implementation plan:
- Stage 1 (this ticket): Implement the detector service and PR runner harness, wire basic artifacts to PR UI. Deliverables: detector binary, runner job image, PR CI integration, docs.
- Stage 2: Nightly baseline job, baseline snapshot store, sliding-window rebaseline logic.
- Stage 3: Dashboarding + automated triage rules + historical anomaly alerts.

Acceptance criteria:
- PR CI correctly flags a synthetic 15% throughput regression in tokens/sec with >95% confidence within N<=20 samples.
- Detector attaches a JSON artifact with raw sample series, test parameters, and a human-readable summary to the PR.
- Nightly baseline updates do not cause immediate block for PRs until an explicit rebaseline review is approved.

Operational notes:
- Runner seeds: use deterministic prompts and fixed random seeds for tokenization/execution to reduce synthetic noise where possible.
- Bucketization: seq-buckets = [<=64, 65-256, 257-1024, >1024]; batch-size buckets tracked separately.
- Hardware labels: cuda-rtx-a100, cuda-rtx-a6000, cpu-x86-skl. Baselines keyed by hardware string.

Risks and mitigations:
- Flaky infra -> false positives: mitigation = require minimum sample size and insist on stable baseline variance; introduce exponential backoff rechecks and escalate to nightly runs before blocking releases.
- Model churn (new models): provide warn-only default for models without a historical baseline and a straightforward rebaseline approval flow for product owners.

Next steps / tasks:
- Create runner docker image and publish to internal registry (Liam) (ETA: 2026-03-05).
- Add SPRT implementation to ci-tools and expose config via YAML per-job (Sofia) (ETA: 2026-03-08).
- Wire PR artifact upload to GitHub Checks API and link the Grafana panel.

Notes on evaluation and metrics:
- Track PR gating false-positive rate and mean detection latency as primary KPIs. Lower is better for both.
- Track CI minutes added per PR and set a performance budget (target: <= 10 extra minutes per PR on median).

Longer-term ideas (not in scope for this ticket):
- Bayesian hierarchical model to share signal across model-family baselines.
- Automatic rollback on detected regressions with canary policy.
- Synthetic traffic replay from production traces to create realistic load profiles.
